# Evidence you can use.

Build the habits to analyse clinical data, judge research fairly, and turn uncertain evidence into thoughtful decisions.

<div class="hero-actions">
  <a href="S1_T01_DescribingData/index.html">Start with Topic 1</a>

## One course, two connected questions

Semester 1 develops a practical statistical language for analysing clinical data. Semester 2 uses that language to ask whether evidence is trustworthy, meaningful, and applicable.

::: {.playbook-intro}
### This is your REBM playbook

Use it to move from a clinical uncertainty to a defensible conclusion—and to know when the evidence cannot support one. Each completed topic combines concise theory, worked clinical reasoning, reproducible R, common traps, reporting language, and questions for your laboratory book.

<div class="playbook-route">
<div><span>1</span><strong>Frame</strong><small>Name the population, question, outcome, and decision.</small></div>
<div><span>2</span><strong>Describe</strong><small>Understand the data before modelling them.</small></div>
<div><span>3</span><strong>Estimate</strong><small>Keep magnitude and uncertainty together.</small></div>
<div><span>4</span><strong>Challenge</strong><small>Test assumptions, bias, and alternative explanations.</small></div>
<div><span>5</span><strong>Apply</strong><small>Translate evidence into a patient-centred action.</small></div>
</div>
:::

## The weekly rhythm

::: {.fourfold}
<div><strong>Expert case study</strong>A modern clinical problem grounds the week in a real decision.</div>
<div><strong>Theory</strong>Short explanations build a consistent conceptual foundation.</div>
<div><strong>Code-along</strong>Follow an analysis from question to clinically meaningful interpretation.</div>
<div><strong>Tutorial-lab</strong>Adapt the workflow, make a decision, and add to your lab book.</div>
:::

## Five habits to carry into every topic

::: {.habit-grid}
<div><strong>Keep the question visible</strong><span>A method is only useful when it estimates or tests something clinically meaningful.</span></div>
<div><strong>Describe before modelling</strong><span>Data quality, distributions, missingness, and subgroups shape every later conclusion.</span></div>
<div><strong>Report magnitude with uncertainty</strong><span>A p-value, model score, or category cannot replace an effect estimate and its plausible range.</span></div>
<div><strong>Interrogate the assumptions</strong><span>Ask what the analysis needs to be true and what bias would do to the result.</span></div>
<div><strong>Return to the patient</strong><span>Population evidence informs—but never mechanically determines—an individual decision.</span></div>
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Assessment connection

The same habits support the laboratory book, lay evidence summary, group replication report, and individual reflection: make the question explicit, preserve a reproducible trail, interpret rather than copy output, and be honest about what the evidence can and cannot support.
:::
